subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Sarika, it's Sachin, and I have to say this out loud once. In the corridor before assembly, Nikhil and his group kept grabbing my bag and throwing it around, calling me names. There were maybe thirty people there. Some stared at their phones, some looked at the floor, and two laughed. Not one said stop. That silence felt worse than the names. I felt like a piece of furniture. You were the only one who found me at the water tap, and you did not ask anything, you just sat there. Then you said, "Come with me to the counsellor." She listened, said it was not my fault, and called my class teacher and my family that same afternoon.

qa.q: About how many people were in the corridor?
qa.a: There were maybe thirty people in the corridor.

qa.q: Why did the silence feel worse than the names to Sachin?
qa.a: The silence made Sachin feel alone and invisible, like a piece of furniture, as if nobody saw the harm as real.

qa.q: What turning point helped Sachin that day?
qa.a: Sarika sat quietly at the water tap and then took Sachin to the counsellor, who listened, said it was not Sachin's fault, and called the class teacher and family that afternoon.

qa.q: What might Sarika have been feeling when finding Sachin at the water tap and sitting without asking anything?
qa.a: Sarika probably felt concerned and unsure what to say, and chose company over questions so that Sachin would not feel pushed.

grounding: A student being harassed notices that many people see it and nobody speaks; the silence hurts, and an adult responds the same day.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: My name is Chandrika, and I saw it on the school bus home. Two boys in the back seat kept flicking paper balls at Sangeeta and calling out about her hair. The bus was full, maybe twenty-five of us. Nobody said a word. A few people put in earphones and turned to the window. Sangeeta pressed her forehead to the glass and hugged her bag, and her shoulders shrank a little more at every stop. I felt frozen in my seat too. At the market stop I made myself stand up, sat down beside her and called Mrs Rao, the bus attendant, to the back. Mrs Rao moved the boys to the front, stayed near Sangeeta for the rest of the ride and phoned the principal, who said the boys' families would be called that evening. Sangeeta did not say much, but she let me keep the seat.

qa.q: Where did the boys pick on Sangeeta?
qa.a: On the school bus home, where two boys in the back seat flicked paper balls at Sangeeta and called out about her hair.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have been feeling with her forehead pressed to the glass?
qa.a: Sangeeta was probably humiliated and alone; hugging her bag and shrinking at every stop suggests the silence of the full bus hurt as much as the boys' words.

qa.q: What turning point came at the market stop?
qa.a: Chandrika stood up, sat beside Sangeeta and called Mrs Rao, who moved the boys, stayed near Sangeeta and phoned the principal.

qa.q: What was it like for Chandrika to sit frozen while the paper balls kept flying?
qa.a: Chandrika seems to have felt stuck and uneasy, part of the silent crowd, until standing up broke that silence.

grounding: A student being picked on sees a whole bus watch in silence, and a fellow passenger's account shows how that silence isolates her until someone steps in and adults respond the same day.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
The local bus from the village to the college town was packed, as always. Tushar and his two friends stood behind Jaya, making comments about her plait and tugging her dupatta.
Jaya looked around. The conductor was counting coins. Two women from her village were looking out of the window. A man in a white cap stared straight ahead. Twenty people, and not one of them turned.
She held her bag against her chest and stared at the floor, face burning. What hurt most was not the tugging. It was the silence, like she wasn't there.
At home that evening she told Amma. Amma held her, said it was not her fault, and walked with her to the headmaster's house before dark to report the boys.

qa.q: What did Tushar and his friends tug?
qa.a: They tugged her dupatta.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling as she stared at the floor?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and alone, hurt most by the silence of the twenty people who didn't turn.

qa.q: How did Amma respond, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She held Jaya, said it wasn't her fault and reported the boys that same evening, so Jaya didn't feel alone any more.

qa.q: How might one of the village women feel if she later learned what Jaya went through?
qa.a: She might feel ashamed and sorry for looking away, realising her silence added to Jaya's hurt.

grounding: Shows a student harassed on a bus who notices many people see it and nobody speaks, and feels the silence as the deepest hurt.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
In the hallway of their Berlin school, Valentina's friends started again. They imitated Jamal's accent, loud enough for the whole corridor. One knocked his cap off.
Jamal looked around. At least fifteen students. Some laughed. Most looked at their phones. His lab partner, Lukas, turned and walked into a classroom.
Jamal picked up his cap. He wasn't thinking about the girls any more. He was thinking about Lukas's back.
The school librarian, Frau Weber, saw him come in with shaking hands. She sat with him, listened, and said, “This is not your fault.” She walked him to the counsellor's office before the next bell and called his father that afternoon.

qa.q: What did one of the girls knock off?
qa.a: One knocked his cap off.

qa.q: What does Jamal thinking about Lukas's back suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt betrayed and alone; his friend's silence hurt more than the teasing itself.

qa.q: What did Frau Weber do that others could learn from?
qa.a: She listened, told Jamal it was not his fault, took him to the counsellor and called his father the same day.

qa.q: Why might Lukas have walked away?
qa.a: Lukas may have felt scared or unsure what to do, assuming someone else would step in, without seeing how much it hurt Jamal.

grounding: Shows a student harassed in a hallway who notices many watch in silence, and finds that silence hurts more than the act.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
In the computer lab, Mrs Pillai had stepped out for printouts. Varun and his two friends started again. "Sahil, say 'computer' for us. Go on." They copied the way he said it. Someone pressed a sticky note on his back: LOADING...
Sahil looked along the rows of screens. Fifteen classmates. A few grinned. Most stared at their monitors, typing nothing. Nobody said stop. That was what pressed on his chest: not Varun's voice, but fifteen quiet heads. So I'm on my own here, he thought.
When Mrs Pillai came back, Pooja walked straight to her desk and spoke quietly, pointing. Mrs Pillai came over, peeled the note off Sahil's back and said, "Varun, you three stay after class. Sahil, sit with me at break. I'll speak to your class teacher and call home today."
Sahil hadn't expected anyone to speak. Pooja gave him a small nod.

qa.q: What did the sticky note on Sahil's back say?
qa.a: LOADING...

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling as he looked along the silent rows of screens?
qa.a: Sahil felt most hurt and alone because of the fifteen silent classmates; their silence made him believe he was on his own.

qa.q: What did Mrs Pillai's response get right?
qa.a: She removed the note, named the boys, kept Sahil close at break and passed it on to his class teacher and home the same day.

qa.q: What might it have taken for Pooja to walk to Mrs Pillai's desk?
qa.a: Pooja may have felt nervous going against a silent room, but decided Sahil mattered more than blending in.

grounding: Shows a student being teased while a roomful of classmates watches silently, and how that silence makes him feel alone.
